title: How to use this guide
heading: How to read this guide
label: How to read this
summary: Four kinds of statement, and the reading discipline the rest of the guide assumes.

spans.text: The podcast moves unusually fast because both speakers compress several industries into one shorthand. When they say "a gigawatt of compute," they are simultaneously talking about electricity, accelerator performance, a cluster, a data-center site, contracts, and an economic claim. When they say "CapEx," they may move between the chip-factory layer, the server layer, the building layer, and the power-plant layer. The first skill is therefore not memorizing acronyms. It is learning to keep the layers and units separate.
Read Chapters 1-3 and the episode map. Your goal is to recognize the nouns and units.
Read Chapters 4-8 with a pencil. Recalculate the worked examples. Your goal is to understand how physical capacity becomes revenue and how the build is financed.

Read Chapters 9-12. Your goal is to identify what must be true for the podcast's forecasts to hold, what could break the chain, and which statements are accounting identities versus contestable assumptions.
Whenever you encounter a number, ask five questions:
Is it a stock at a date or a flow per year?
Is it electrical power, energy, peak arithmetic performance, or useful delivered work?
Is it owned capacity, leased capacity, or capacity serving a company's models?
Is the money revenue, gross profit, operating profit, cash flow, or asset value?
Is it observed, estimated, contracted, forecast, or a thought experiment?

UNIT DISCIPLINE. The single most important reading habit is to restore the denominator. "$15 million per megawatt" is incomplete unless you know whether it means per MW-year of reserved IT capacity, a one-time construction cost, or annual revenue. The surrounding discussion strongly suggests annualized capacity economics in many places, but the transcript does not state the convention every time.
